summary: LoST maps a location and a service type, such as emergency help, to the right service contact. This experimental extension lets a client ask a LoST server which services it offers for a location and also learn the boundary of the area covered. That gives the client context to cache results sensibly and avoid needless queries.

eli5.summary: You ask a switchboard who answers emergencies where you are. This extension also lets the switchboard tell you how far its answer is good for, so you needn't ask again after each step.

subtitle: Tells clients the geographic limits of available services to avoid missing new options.

tldr.problem: LoST helps find services like emergency numbers by location, but when a client queries which services are available, the server does not say how far that list is valid. A moving client might miss a new service becoming available.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds a Service List Boundary to LoST responses. The server tells the client the geographic region within which the returned service list does not change, so the client only needs to re-query when it leaves that boundary.
tldr.outcome: Clients can efficiently track service availability when moving without repeatedly querying the server, and they will not miss new services appearing in their area.

today: RFC 6197 is an Experimental specification published by the IETF. It extends the LoST protocol with Service List Boundary support. The extension is backward-compatible and designed to improve efficiency and reliability for mobile emergency service discovery.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) is a protocol that maps a location and a service type to a URI where you can reach that service—for example, the emergency number for your area. LoST already has a Service Boundary feature that tells clients the region where a particular service (like police) has the same contact number.

However, LoST also has a query called listServicesByLocation that tells a client what services are available at a location. The problem is that the response does not include context: the client learns which services exist, but not how far that list remains valid. If a mobile client learns that services A, B, and C are available in one area, moves to a neighboring region, and only continues to refresh the mappings for A, B, and C, it will not discover that service D has become available. This extension adds a Service List Boundary to solve this problem.
sections.eli5: LoST helps you find emergency numbers. The old way just told you which numbers exist where you are. The new extension also says: this list of services is good throughout this whole region.

sections.title: How the Extension Works
sections.content:
A client making a listServicesByLocation query can now include an optional serviceListBoundaryRequest element, asking for boundary information. The server responds with the service list as before, but also includes a serviceListBoundary element that describes the geographic region (using civic or geodetic location format) within which that service list is valid and includes an expires time.

The boundary information can be returned in two ways. The by value approach includes the boundary geometry directly in the response. The by reference approach returns a reference key that the client can later use to fetch the boundary details via a new getServiceListBoundary query, similar to how Service Boundaries work in the base LoST protocol.

The boundary is uniquely identified by a serviceListKey, a random token with at least 128 bits of entropy. When the boundary changes, a new key is assigned. The server may return multiple boundary representations for different location profiles (civic and geodetic), but must use at least one profile the client used in its request.
sections.eli5: The response says: these services are the same everywhere within Lower Austria (or another region). When you leave that region, ask again. You can ask for the boundary details right away or get a key to look them up later.

sections.title: Client and Server Implementation
sections.content:
On the server side, a LoST forest guide (the component that aggregates service coverage information) has enough information to compute the Service List Boundary because it knows all the services and their individual coverage regions. The calculation of the exact largest area where a service list remains unchanged can be complex, so servers may choose to return smaller, easier-to-compute areas. For example, a server might use regional administrative boundaries (counties, states, cantons) as Service List Boundaries even if some adjacent regions offer the same services. The key requirement is that the boundary must be small enough that a moving client will detect any change in available services.

On the client side, a mobile LoST implementation that already handles Service Boundaries needs only minor changes to support Service List Boundaries. When the client moves, it checks whether it has left the Service List Boundary. If it has, the client performs a new listServicesByLocation query to learn about any new services. If it has not left the boundary, the client already knows the service list has not changed, so it only needs to refresh mappings for the services it previously discovered.
sections.eli5: Servers store information about all services and their areas. They can say when the service list changes. Clients remember the boundary and only ask again when they leave it.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Service List Boundaries are computed by the server from individual Service Boundaries. They are optional; the LoST server may return them or not based on local policy, just like Service Boundaries. The security and privacy considerations are the same as for the base LoST protocol [RFC5222], including access control and confidentiality requirements. No new security measures are required because boundary information has the same sensitivity as Service Boundaries.

The extension is defined in a new XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:lost1:slb. The extension is backward-compatible: older LoST clients will ignore the boundary elements, and older servers can simply omit them. listServices queries (which do not include location) are not extended with boundary information because there is no location context.
sections.eli5: The boundary information is no more sensitive than the service list itself, so the same security rules apply. Older systems can ignore the new information without breaking.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is designed to integrate smoothly into existing LoST deployments. Clients only need to add parsing for the serviceListBoundary and serviceListBoundaryReference elements. The serviceListBoundaryRequest element added to listServicesByLocation is optional, so old clients continue to work.

The getServiceListBoundary query allows clients to fetch boundary details later using the serviceListKey, reducing the size of initial responses when boundaries are large or complex. This is particularly valuable for emergency services (sos.*) where it is crucial that moving clients never miss a change in available services.

The RFC notes that different countries have different administrative structures and service coverage patterns. Some may use county or state lines as boundaries, others may compute boundaries based on actual coverage maps. The standard allows flexibility, requiring only that the boundary be accurate enough to notify clients of service list changes.
sections.eli5: Different places organize services differently, so there is no one right way to draw the boundary. The standard just says it has to be good enough that people moving do not miss a new service.
